articles.title: My form wrote a sentence that wasn't true, and the user would have signed it
articles.description: I built a small page that writes appeal letters for UK private parking tickets. You answer a few...
articles.body_html:
I built a small page that writes appeal letters for UK private parking tickets. You answer a few questions, it produces a letter.

I tested it the way I test most forms. Fill in good data, check the output looks right. Every combination passed: three parts of the UK, keeper or driver, five grounds. No script errors.

Then I did the thing I should have done first. I picked a ground and typed in data that did not support it.

The ground

One of the five grounds is about a deadline. In England and Wales, if a private parking company posts you a ticket and nothing was left on the windscreen, the notice has to be delivered to the registered keeper within 14 days. It's in Schedule 4 of the Protection of Freedoms Act 2012, paragraph 9. People ask about it on forums all the time. Here is one thread where the notice took more than 30 days: https://www.ftla.uk/private-parking-tickets/late-notice-to-keeper-30-days-worth-appealing/

So the form asks for the date of parking and the date the notice arrived.

The bug

I entered a parking date and a received date 7 days apart. Under the field, the helper text did the right thing:

You received it 7 days after the parking date. This ground needs more than 14 days, so it may not apply.

And the letter, a few centimetres to the right, said this:

Your notice is dated 6 October 2026 and I received it on 6 October 2026, which is outside that period.

That sentence is false, and the page wrote it. The person using it is stressed, skims the preview, prints, signs.

The cause was boring. The helper text and the letter were built by two different functions. One compared the dates. The other just filled a template.

The fix

I did not make the letter clever. A letter that silently rewrites its own argument is hard to trust. The page now puts a warning above the letter, next to the count of unfilled fields:

const pd = $('parkDate').value, rd = $('receivedDate').value;
if (radio('ground') === 'keeper' && $('jurisdiction').value === 'EW'
    && pd && rd && daysBetween(pd, rd) <= 14) {
  add('', '<strong>Check your dates.</strong> This letter says the notice ' +
    'arrived more than 14 days after parking, but the dates you entered are ' +
    'within 14 days. Correct the dates or choose a different ground.');
}

The second one

While I was in there I found the letter's date came from this:

new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)

toISOString() is UTC. The UK is an hour ahead of UTC in summer. Between midnight and 1 am the letter would be dated yesterday. Not a disaster, but it is a dated legal letter, and the fix is three lines:

const localIso = d =>
  `${d.getFullYear()}-${String(d.getMonth() + 1).padStart(2, '0')}-${String(d.getDate()).padStart(2, '0')}`;

What I took from it

If a form generates text that a person will sign, test each option with inputs that contradict it. "Does it render" is not the test. "Can it say something untrue" is.

The page is here if you want to poke at it: https://mianazeemdaula.github.io/parking-appeal-letter/
Source: https://github.com/mianazeemdaula/parking-appeal-letter

I'm a developer, not a lawyer, and no solicitor has reviewed the wording. It was tested in headless Chrome only, not on real phones, Safari or Firefox.

articles.title: A pivot table your users can drag, on a million rows, and how to tell whether it freezes the page
articles.description: Every reporting screen gets the same request after its first week: "Can I see this by month instead?"...
articles.body_html:
Every reporting screen gets the same request after its first week: "Can I see this by month instead?" Then by product, then by country and month together. A pivot table is the answer that stops the requests, because the user drags the fields where they want them and gets the report they were about to ask for.

The catch is the data. Every drag regroups and re-sums every row. With a few thousand rows nobody notices. With a million, the obvious implementation freezes the page while it works, and a page that freezes on every drag is a page people stop dragging in.

This post measures that on real data: the 1,067,371 invoice lines of the Online Retail II dataset, pivoted in the browser with our free PivotGrid. The demo times every recompute in your own browser, so you can check each number here against your machine.

The report a user builds

Start from revenue by country and year, then drag Month into the columns or Product into the rows. Each drop recomputes the whole table:

In React that is one component and a list of fields; area says where each field starts, and the user moves them from there:

import { BasePivotGrid } from '@kanunilabs/pivotgrid-react';
import '@kanunilabs/pivotgrid-react/styles.css';

const fields = [
  { id: 'country', dataField: 'country', caption: 'Country', dataType: 'string', area: 'row' },
  { id: 'year', dataField: 'year', caption: 'Year', dataType: 'string', area: 'column' },
  { id: 'revenue', dataField: 'revenue', caption: 'Revenue', dataType: 'number', area: 'data', summaryType: 'sum' },
  { id: 'month', dataField: 'month', caption: 'Month', dataType: 'string', area: 'filter' },  // waiting to be dragged
  { id: 'product', dataField: 'description', caption: 'Product', dataType: 'string', area: 'filter' },
];

<BasePivotGrid gridId="sales" data={rows} initialFields={fields} />;

What a drag costs

The demo measures two things on every recompute:

  • How long it takes, from the moment the pivot starts to the moment the new table is painted.
  • The longest pause on the page's main thread in that window. The browser's Long Tasks API reports every task of 50 ms or more, and the main thread is the one that also handles your clicks and keys. Rendering the new table counts too.

For country by year, or sales against cancellations by country, a recompute took 29 to 48 ms and no task on the main thread reached 50 ms. Drag Month into the columns and Year out, about 40 countries by 25 months, and it took 45 to 82 ms over three runs, with the longest pause between none and 54 ms:

The grouping and summing run in a Web Worker, a second thread the page starts for the pivot. The main thread only receives the finished totals and draws them.

The obvious way, measured

To see what the worker buys, the demo has a button that computes the same country-by-year revenue the way a quick implementation would: one pass over every row with a Map, on the main thread.

const totals = new Map<string, number>();
for (const r of rows) {
  const key = `${r.country}|${r.year}`;
  totals.set(key, (totals.get(key) ?? 0) + r.revenue);
}

That loop froze the page for about 110 ms, longer than the pivot's whole recompute. Its totals are the same as the pivot's: £7,511,064 for the United Kingdom in 2011 and £134,790 for France in 2010, which we also checked with an independent computation over the source file.

A tenth of a second does not sound like much until you type through it. The demo has a text box for that: type while you drag fields, and the letters keep appearing; type while the loop runs, and they arrive all at once when it ends.

The worker does not make the work free. It moves it off the thread that answers the user.

Where the page stopped, and the fix it led to

Put Product in the rows and Month in the columns, about 5,000 products by 25 months, sorted by name, and the measurement changed: on October 7 the recompute took 350 to 650 ms and the main thread paused for 290 to 510 ms.

The aggregation was still in the worker, so we looked at what was left on the main thread. Sorting the same table by revenue instead of by name cut the pause to 105 to 183 ms. The difference was how the 5,000 product names were compared:

// what the pivot's sort did before 1.7.2
names.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, locale, { numeric: true }));

// the same order, with the collator built once
const collator = new Intl.Collator(locale, { numeric: true });
names.sort(collator.compare);

Both give the same order. On 5,000 names, about 60,000 comparisons, the first took 206 to 226 ms and the second 4 to 5 ms, on the same machine. Called with an options object, localeCompare sets up its comparison rules again on every call; a collator sets them up once.

We shipped the second version in PivotGrid 1.7.2 on October 8 (@kanunilabs/pivotgrid-react 1.4.2). Measured again in the live demo, five loads each, the layout sorted by name now takes 151 to 196 ms with a longest pause of 97 to 118 ms, the same as sorted by revenue. You can check it at /demos/pivot?layout=product-month&sort=name.

If you sort strings anywhere a user waits, a table header, a filter list, a dropdown, this one is worth checking in your own code.

The remaining 100 or so milliseconds were in the React grid, not in the pivot. After the first paint it measured the panel widths and header heights and kept them in React state, so the roughly 1,400 visible cells were drawn a second time in the same task, only to change two paddings and a few CSS variables. It also wrote the row-header width variables on the grid's outer box, where every cell inherits them, so each write invalidated the style of every cell and the next measurement forced a full style recalculation. Now the measurements go through refs and the variables sit only on the panel that reads them. On a local production build of this demo, ten switches to Product × Month, the median longest pause went from 89 to 51 ms and the recompute from 155 to 102 ms. That fix shipped in @kanunilabs/pivotgrid-react 1.5.0 on October 9.

Measure your own pivot

You do not need our component to get these two numbers. Any pivot or table that recomputes on user input can be measured the same way:

const longTasks: PerformanceEntry[] = [];
new PerformanceObserver((list) => longTasks.push(...list.getEntries()))
  .observe({ type: 'longtask', buffered: true });

const t0 = performance.now();
await recompute();                       // whatever your table does on a drag
requestAnimationFrame(() => requestAnimationFrame(() => {
  const t1 = performance.now();          // the new table has been painted
  const pause = Math.max(0, ...longTasks
    .filter((t) => t.startTime + t.duration >= t0 && t.startTime <= t1)
    .map((t) => t.duration));
  console.log(`recompute ${t1 - t0} ms, longest main-thread pause ${pause} ms`);
}));

If the second number is large, your users feel it, whatever the first one says.

What this costs

  • It is free. Drag and drop, filters, sorting, % of totals and saved views are in the Community package, with no licence key and no watermark. Calculated fields in code and the rows behind a clicked cell are free too; the formula designer for end users, rendered charts, the ready-made drill-down window and styled Excel/PDF export are in the paid edition.
  • The data has to be in the browser. The demo downloads a 5.5 MB file once and decodes it into a million row objects before the first pivot. For data that should stay on the server, the paid edition can ask your server for the aggregates instead.
  • Wide layouts still pause the page. For 5,000 products by 25 months, after the two fixes above, the median longest pause was 51 ms on our local production build; slower machines see more. The panel in the demo shows what yours does.

Try it

The demo is at /demos/pivot; /demos/pivot?layout=product-month opens the wide layout, best sellers first, and adding &sort=name sorts it by name. The PivotGrid docs cover fields, filters, summary types and the React and plain JavaScript setups.

Data: Online Retail II, UCI Machine Learning Repository (Chen, 2019), CC BY 4.0.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance. The demo and every number in it were measured against our packages and the published dataset in October 2026.

articles.title: TrailWhistle: A Bird-Call Identifier That Works With Zero Bars of Signal
articles.description: TrailWhistle runs the open-source BirdNET model entirely on your phone: 6,522 species, no internet, no account, no cloud.
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

What I Built

Last spring I was on a trail at dawn, that electric half-hour when every bird in the forest is shouting at once, and I realized I could name maybe three of them. My phone had no signal, and the bird apps I knew about needed the cloud. So I just stood there, surrounded by a symphony I couldn't understand.

That frustration became TrailWhistle: point your phone at the dawn chorus and it tells you who's singing, using AI that runs entirely on your device. It listens to 3 seconds of birdsong and identifies the species, with common name, scientific name, and confidence score. No internet. No account. No data leaving your phone.

It's also a small biodiversity survey tool. Visit a park repeatedly and it builds a living checklist of every species detected there, each with timestamps and GPS coordinates, exportable as CSV or JSON. Over a season, you watch your local patch come alive on paper.

Who it's for: the hiker who hears something amazing and wants a name for it, the parent whose kid asks "what's that bird?", the gardener curious about who's visiting, and anyone who has stood in the woods surrounded by sound and wanted to understand it.

How it gets you off the screen: the design goal is that the screen is the shortest part of your day. Three seconds of recording, phone back in your pocket, eyes on the canopy.

Demo

Try it live: https://trailwhistle.onrender.com

Tap one of the demo calls (American Robin, Song Sparrow, Mourning Dove, Barn Owl) to see the full detection flow, or open the Species tab and search all 6,522 species BirdNET knows.

Even better: take your phone outside tomorrow morning and tap record on a real bird.

Code

Sourabh-Kumar04 / TrailWhistle

Offline-first bird-call identifier PWA with on-device open-weight AI

🌿 TrailWhistle

Offline-first, on-device Area Biodiversity Survey Tool & Avian Census PWA.
Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 1 (Theme: "Touch Grass").
Zero cloud servers. Zero API keys. Zero cellular data required.

📖 Overview

TrailWhistle gets people off the screen and into the natural world. In remote wilderness, mountain canyons, and deep forests, cellular reception drops to zero. That's usually where traditional AI applications fail.

TrailWhistle is architected as an Area Biodiversity Survey Tool running 100% on-device using the open-weight BirdNET v2.4 ONNX model (6,522 global avian species) compiled to WebAssembly via ONNX Runtime Web (onnxruntime-web).

Rather than isolated single-bird identification, TrailWhistle supports the core ecological field workflow:

  1. Arrive at a location: Set your survey site (e.g. Pine Ridge Trailhead, Redwood Creek Basin) and habitat transect.
  2. Sample continuously: Tap once to capture 3 seconds of birdsong across the area as calls…
View on GitHub

MIT licensed. React + TypeScript PWA. The interesting parts are src/services/classifier.ts (the inference pipeline) and public/inference-worker.js (the Web Worker that keeps the UI smooth during classification).

How I Built It

The heart of TrailWhistle is BirdNET v2.4, the open bioacoustic model from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Chemnitz University of Technology, trained on recordings contributed by birders and researchers to community archives such as xeno-canto.

  1. Capture. An AudioWorklet grabs microphone input at 48 kHz, BirdNET's required sample rate, and slices it into 3-second windows. There's a ScriptProcessor fallback for older browsers.
  2. On-device inference. The model (~47 MB, ONNX format) runs through onnxruntime-web with WebAssembly SIMD acceleration, inside a Web Worker. No server, no API key, no round trip. It looks at 144,000 audio samples and outputs confidence scores for all 6,522 species.
  3. Honest results. Below 25% confidence, the app says "Unknown" instead of guessing. An earlier version of this project fabricated species names when confidence was low, and I ripped that out. In a field tool, a wrong answer is worse than no answer.
  4. Offline-first. A service worker caches the app shell, the model weights, and the taxonomy. The first visit downloads ~50 MB; after that, airplane mode is fine. The field log persists to localStorage with GPS coordinates.

The whole thing is a PWA, so you can install it from the browser and it lives on your home screen like a native app.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open weights make four properties true at the same time, and a closed API would struggle to offer all of them together:

  • It works where there's no signal. The best birding spots have none. A closed API needs a connection for every identification. With open weights, the model lives on the device after one download.
  • It's private by architecture. Every 3-second clip is stamped with GPS. Sent to a cloud API, that's a map of everywhere you hike. With local inference, audio and location never leave the phone: no account, no tracking, no telemetry.
  • There's no per-use cost. Identifying 1,000 birds costs nothing extra, which matters for a free tool whose whole point is getting kids and casual hikers into nature. (BirdNET's model is released under a Creative Commons non-commercial license, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so TrailWhistle stays free and non-commercial, with attribution to the BirdNET team.)
  • It's swappable, not rented. The model is standard ONNX. When BirdNET updates, or someone fine-tunes a model for a particular region, I replace one file. No vendor can change pricing or deprecate an endpoint out from under the app.

And it's open all the way down: community-contributed recordings, an open model, an open runtime, and an MIT-licensed app that anyone can fork tonight.

My Agent Session

I built this with AI coding agents as pair programmers: architecture decisions, implementation, test suites, and many rounds of UI iteration driven by real browser screenshots.

The most valuable thing the agents did wasn't writing code. It was the hostile review loop. After each build, an agent played a harsh hackathon judge in a real browser and caught real failures, including a silent inference pipeline that looked fine in unit tests but produced nothing in the browser. The same loop caught the old code inventing species names at low confidence, and the fix wasn't a tweak but a principle: never fabricate, always admit uncertainty.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Render: TrailWhistle is deployed and hosted on Render (https://trailwhistle.onrender.com), which serves the PWA, the BirdNET model files, and the full 6,522-species taxonomy.

Tomorrow morning, before the sun is fully up, open the app and tap record. The screen should be the shortest part of your day.

articles.title: 5 JavaScript Bugs That Look Correct (But Absolutely Are Not)
articles.description: Every one of the snippets below looks fine. Clean, short, reasonable. The kind of code you'd nod at...
articles.body_html:
Every one of the snippets below looks fine. Clean, short, reasonable. The kind of code you'd nod at in a review and move on.

And every single one is broken.

I've run each of these in Node to confirm — no tricks, no outdated browser quirks. Just JavaScript being JavaScript. Let's go through them one by one: the code, what you'd expect, what actually happens, and the fix.

Bug 1: ['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)

This one looks like the most natural code in the world. You've got strings, you want numbers, parseInt converts strings to numbers. What could go wrong?

const numbers = ['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt);
console.log(numbers);
// You'd expect: [1, 2, 3]

What you actually get:

[1, NaN, NaN]

Wait, what? The first one works and the rest explode?

Here's the catch: map doesn't call your function with one argument. It calls it with three — the element, the index, and the whole array. And parseInt doesn't take one argument either. It takes two — the string, and the radix (the number base).

So what really happens is:

parseInt('1', 0)  // radix 0 = "figure it out yourself" → 1 ✓
parseInt('2', 1)  // radix 1 = not a real number base → NaN ✗
parseInt('3', 2)  // "3" isn't a valid digit in base 2 → NaN ✗

The array index silently becomes the number base. Beautiful. Terrible.

The fix — wrap it so parseInt only ever sees what you intend:

const numbers = ['1', '2', '3'].map(n => parseInt(n, 10));
// [1, 2, 3] ✓

The lesson: never pass a multi-argument function directly into map, filter, or forEach. They always sneak extra arguments in.

Bug 2: [10, 9, 80].sort()

Sorting numbers. Can't mess that up, right?

const scores = [10, 9, 80].sort();
console.log(scores);
// You'd expect: [9, 10, 80]

What you actually get:

[10, 80, 9]

JavaScript's default sort() doesn't compare numbers. It converts everything to strings first, then sorts alphabetically. And alphabetically, "10" comes before "80" comes before "9" — because "1" < "8" < "9". It's sorting words, not values.

The fix — tell it how to compare:

const scores = [10, 9, 80].sort((a, b) => a - b);
// [9, 10, 80] ✓

The lesson: sort() without a compare function is almost never what you want for numbers. This one has bitten literally everyone at least once.

Bug 3: 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3

Quick sanity check. One tenth plus two tenths equals three tenths. First-grade math.

console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);
// You'd expect: true

What you actually get:

false

Because:

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);
// 0.30000000000000004

Computers store decimals in binary floating point, and some perfectly innocent-looking decimals — like 0.1 — can't be represented exactly in binary. It's like trying to write 1/3 in decimal: 0.3333... forever. The tiny leftover error accumulates, and your "equal" comparison fails.

This isn't even JavaScript-specific — Python, Java, and C all do the same thing. It's just how floats work.

The fix — don't compare floats directly. Compare with a tiny tolerance:

const EPSILON = 0.000001;
console.log(Math.abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < EPSILON);
// true ✓

Or round to the decimals you actually care about before comparing.

The lesson: never trust === with decimal math. If money is involved, work in cents (integers), not dollars (floats).

Bug 4: typeof null === 'object'

This one is a fossil — a bug so old it's basically a feature now.

console.log(typeof null);
// You'd expect: "null"
// What you get: "object"

Why? In the very first version of JavaScript, values were stored with a small "type tag" in front of them. Objects had tag 0. And null was represented as a null pointer — which is all zeros. So null accidentally wore the "object" nametag, and the check has returned 'object' ever since, for almost 30 years.

Fixing it now would break half the internet, so it stays. Forever.

This bites you in real code like this:

function process(data) {
  if (typeof data === 'object') {
    console.log(Object.keys(data)); // 💥 TypeError if data is null
  }
}
process(null);

The fix — always pair the check with an explicit null guard:

if (data !== null && typeof data === 'object') {
  // safe now ✓
}

The lesson: typeof tells you the category, not the value. And null has been lying about its category since 1995.

Bug 5: await inside forEach doesn't wait

This is the sneakiest one on the list, because the await keyword is right there. It looks like it must work.

async function saveAll(items) {
  items.forEach(async (item) => {
    await saveToDatabase(item);
  });
  console.log('All saved!');
}

saveAll([1, 2, 3]);

You'd expect: save 1, save 2, save 3, then print "All saved!"

What actually happens: "All saved!" prints first, while the saves are still running. I confirmed it — the log fires before any item finishes.

Why? forEach doesn't know or care about promises. It calls your async function, gets a promise back, and throws it on the floor. It never awaits anything. Your await inside the callback only pauses that one callback — the loop itself blasts through all items instantly and moves on.

The fix — use a for...of loop, which actually respects await:

async function saveAll(items) {
  for (const item of items) {
    await saveToDatabase(item);
  }
  console.log('All saved!'); // now this really runs last ✓
}

(Need them to run in parallel instead? Use await Promise.all(items.map(...)) — that's the deliberate version of what forEach pretends to do.)

The lesson: forEach + async is a trap. The await inside looks like it controls the loop. It doesn't.

The pattern

Look at all five together and a pattern emerges: every bug comes from JavaScript quietly doing something adjacent to what you asked for. Extra arguments slipped into your function. Strings sorted instead of numbers. Binary approximations instead of decimals. A 30-year-old type tag. A loop that ignores your promises.

The code looks correct because each line is reasonable in isolation. The bug lives in what JavaScript does behind the line.

The best defense isn't memorizing gotchas — it's running the code and looking at the actual output. Every result in this post came from a real Node run, not from memory. When something "should work" but doesn't, console.log the intermediate values. The answer is usually one step away from where you're looking.

Which of these has bitten you before? And what's the worst "looks correct" bug you've shipped? I'm collecting them.
